# firecrawl scrape

Scrape one or more URLs. Returns clean, LLM-optimized markdown. Multiple URLs are scraped concurrently.

## Quick start

```bash
# Basic markdown extraction
firecrawl scrape "<url>" -o .firecrawl/page.md

# Main content only, no nav/footer
firecrawl scrape "<url>" --only-main-content -o .firecrawl/page.md

# Wait for JS to render, then scrape
firecrawl scrape "<url>" --wait-for 3000 -o .firecrawl/page.md

# Multiple URLs (markdown only; each saved to .firecrawl/; -o is ignored)
firecrawl scrape https://example.com https://example.com/blog https://example.com/docs

# Get markdown and links together
firecrawl scrape "<url>" --format markdown,links -o .firecrawl/page.json

# Ask a question about the page
firecrawl scrape "https://example.com/pricing" --query "What is the enterprise plan price?"
```

Run `firecrawl scrape --help` for the full option list.

**Done when:** you have the scraped content — on stdout, in your `-o` file, or under `.firecrawl/` for multi-URL scrapes — and have inspected it with bounded reads (`head`, `grep`) to answer the request.

## Tips

- **Prefer plain scrape over `--query`.** Scrape to a file, then use `grep`, `head`, or read the markdown directly — you can search and reason over the full content yourself. Use `--query` only when you want a single targeted answer without saving the page (costs 5 extra credits).
- **Scrape handles static pages and JS-rendered SPAs.** Escalate to `interact` when the page needs interaction (clicks, form fills, pagination) or scrape misses content.
- Multiple URLs are scraped concurrently — check `firecrawl --status` for your concurrency limit. This mode saves markdown only and ignores `-o`; other requested formats are dropped. If markdown wasn't requested, the whole JSON response is written into the `.md` file.
- Single format outputs raw content. Multiple formats (e.g., `--format markdown,links`) output JSON.
- Always quote URLs — shell interprets `?` and `&` as special characters.
- Naming convention: `.firecrawl/{site}-{path}.md`

## See also

- [firecrawl-search](../firecrawl-search/SKILL.md) — find pages when you don't have a URL
- [firecrawl-interact](../firecrawl-interact/SKILL.md) — when scrape can't get the content, use `interact` to click, fill forms, etc.
- [firecrawl-download](../firecrawl-download/SKILL.md) — bulk download an entire site to local files
- [firecrawl-build-scrape](https://github.com/firecrawl/skills/tree/main/skills/build/firecrawl-build-scrape) — building scrape into an app instead of running it here

From the back of the book:
Build semantic knowledge systems with trusted and AI-ready taxonomies, ontologies, and knowledge graphs.

Ontology Pipeline gives data leaders, semantic engineers, ontologists, taxonomists, knowledge managers, librarians, AI architects, and enterprise data teams a practical framework for turning messy organizational language into structured, machine-readable knowledge. Instead of treating ontology development or knowledge graph construction as a black box, this book provides a clear sequence: controlled vocabularies, metadata schemas, taxonomies, thesauri, ontologies, and knowledge graphs.

Analyze how language, definitions, labels, synonyms, metadata, and relationships shape the performance of artificial intelligence systems. The book explains why large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, semantic search, entity resolution, and information retrieval all depend on clean, governed, semantically enriched data. It also shows how library and information science methods can help organizations build scalable semantic knowledge management systems that support both human understanding and machine reasoning.

Design each stage of the Ontology Pipeline with practical guidance, examples, standards, and implementation patterns. Readers will explore controlled vocabulary development, SKOS taxonomies, thesaurus relationships, RDF, OWL, SHACL, SPARQL, competency questions, ontology governance, semantic validation, and knowledge graph architecture. The book connects these concepts to real enterprise needs, including data quality, semantic layers, AI governance, domain modeling, knowledge management, and production AI infrastructure.

Evaluate what it really takes to build and maintain a knowledge graph as architecture, not just as a product or database. Learn why we build, govern, and maintain a knowledge graph with attention to semantic debt, staffing, operational funding, ontology change management, validation workflows, and long-term trust. For teams investing in AI, data governance, data catalogs, metadata management, enterprise architecture, or semantic technology, this book provides the missing roadmap.

Apply the Ontology Pipeline to create a formal, explicit, shared model of what your organization knows. Whether you are building a semantic layer, improving RAG accuracy, designing a domain ontology, creating an enterprise knowledge graph, or trying to make AI outputs more reliable, Ontology Pipeline provides the vocabulary, structure, and processes to move from disconnected data to governed organizational knowledge.

One of the biggest shifts happening in our industry is that enterprise data management is expanding into enterprise knowledge management. AI is accelerating that transition because it depends on more than well-managed data. It depends upon context, shared meaning, trusted relationships, and the ability to organize the vast stores of unstructured knowledge that exist across every large enterprise. As AI becomes the primary interface to enterprise information, knowledge management will become the foundation that unlocks trustworthy AI at scale.

What’s inside the Studio?
The studio has two complete pipeline builds:

The Special Solutions workflows example from the Ontology Pipeline book

Two use cases, each markedly different, but both structured end-to-end using the Ontology Pipeline framework. From controlled vocabularies, to metadata schemas, the process follows onwards with taxonomy, thesaurus, ontology and finally, a fully realized, queryable knowledge graph.

The tool is interactive, and your participation is encouraged. Readers can add concepts, classes, properties and relations. The idea is to solidify your own understanding and skills, solidifying and reinforcing your own understanding of each stage of building a semantic knowledge infrastructure.

Worried About Breaking the Model?
Go ahead a break the system!

Test the boundaries and receive feedback from the tool, when an added element does not validate or conform to the standards encoded within the Studio. Own your learning journey and don’t be afraid to make mistakes. It is from mistakes that the greatest learning happens.

Give the Ontology Pipeline Studio a try 🧱

Ontology Pipeline Studio

A SKOS Taxonomy and Thesaurus Editor, Built from Standards
Intentional Arrangement is a SKOS taxonomy editor that opens as a single static page in your web browser. There is no account, server, or upload. You write concepts, labels, definitions, and relationships; the editor validates them as you type and exports the result to Turtle, RDF/XML, JSON-LD, RDF/JSON, CSV, Excel, and Markdown.

The Intentional Arrangement SKOS Editor is live at https://jesstalisman-ia.github.io/intentional-arrangement-skos/ and the source is public at https://github.com/jesstalisman-ia/intentional-arrangement-skos.




The Origin of the Editor

I built this inside a larger toolset I use for client vocabulary work, then pulled the SKOS portion out so folks could use it on its own. The working model follows W3C SKOS and SKOS-XL, Dublin Core for scheme metadata, and ISO 25964, the international standard for thesauri and interoperability with other vocabularies.




Every concept gets a URI, one preferred label per language, alternate and hidden labels, the full set of SKOS notes, and as many broader concepts as the vocabulary requires. Collections and ordered collections sit beside the hierarchy without being mistaken for it. Language tags follow BCP 47.

Validation inside the edit loop
Vocabulary problems get expensive once the vocabulary ships. The editor applies the qSKOS quality criteria (Mader, Haslhofer and Isaac, 2012) while you are still editing: orphan concepts, missing labels, cyclic hierarchies, and the rest of the checklist surface in the workspace, and most come with a one-click fix.

Work stays in your browser
Projects autosave to local browser storage. From there you can export, download a workspace backup, or generate a read-only share link that packs the whole taxonomy inside the URL for business reviewers. Teams whose vocabularies outgrow a URL can connect an optional Apache Jena Fuseki server and publish each project to its own named graph. Clearing browser data erases local work, so export regularly.




Keep the editorial judgment
The editor is for people anyone wanting to build a standards-based RDF controlled vocabulary, taxonomy, and thesaurus. Plain language queries use offline rules, and nothing in the browser editor calls a language model. An optional REST API handles validation and conversion for teams with their own pipelines, and an MCP server exposes the same functions to assistant tools.

The license with a size threshold
Organizations with fewer than 75 employees may use, modify, and redistribute the editor free under Apache 2.0 as modified by the size-based licensing notice. Organizations with 75 or more employees need a written enterprise license before use; inquiries go to Hello@ontologypipeline.com. The taxonomies you build are yours.

Several recent releases came directly from GitHub issues so feedback, feature requests, and use cases are greatly appreciated!

Good news: the repo already sits on most of this catalog's foundation. Here's the diff after checking every section of the list against `LIONG-REF-001` and the package.

## Already covered — no action

- **W3C core**: RDF, RDFS, SKOS, OWL 2, PROV-O, OWL-Time, SHACL — all in the register and LIONG-006/007.
- **Tooling already assessed**: pySHACL (validator), Apache Jena/Fuseki.
- **Skills sources**: ESCO, NICE Framework, DOL skills taxonomy — already the LIONG-005 shortlist.
- **Methods already in the design**: identity resolution/authority control and crosswalks (LIONG-006/009), FAIR-style governance (LIONG-015).

## Genuinely new and useful — mapped to the doc that owns each kind

| Candidate from the catalog | What it gives this repo | Where it would land |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **SSSOM** — tabular standard for exchanging ontology mappings with provenance | The register's whole model of "reviewed mappings" is otherwise unstandardized; this is the natural format | LIONG-005/007 (mapping artifacts, OI-13) |
| **qSKOS** (26 computable SKOS quality issues), **Skosify**, **SKOS Play!**, **SHACL Playground** | Concrete quality checks for any taxonomy the skills pilot adopts | LIONG-005 source assessment; LIONG-011 toolchain |
| **ISO 25964-1/2, ANSI/NISO Z39.19, SKOS-Thes** | The vocabulary-construction and mapping standards behind SKOS practice — grounds the taxonomy-construction method | `guideline_to_map_ontology_to_LPG`, OI-13 |
| **Neo4j neosemantics (n10s), Ontop, RML/R2RML engines** | The RDF→graph path the `guideline_to_map_ontology_to_LPG` folder covers; n10s is the plugin for exactly that projection | LIONG-011/012 |
| **RDF-star / RDF 1.2 (triple terms)** | Statements-about-statements — an alternative to the repo's record-version-ID pattern for rating/decision provenance | LIONG-006/007 (assess against the existing pattern, not necessarily adopt) |
| **JSON-LD 1.1, DCMI Terms, W3CDTF** | API-friendly serialization and date-format conventions | LIONG-007/011 |
| **Oxigraph** | Embeddable SPARQL store as a lighter alternative alongside Jena Fuseki | LIONG-011 |
| **BARTOC, LOV, LOD Cloud, BioPortal** | Registries to search before building any vocabulary from scratch — matches the register's "where to look" rule | LIONG-005 discovery |
| **Skosmos, WebVOWL, SemSpect, the IA SKOS editor** | Public UI/visualization options for browsing the graph and vocabulary | LIONG-014 |
| **KG-LLM literature** — Allemang & Sequeda (ISWC 2024, ontologies raising LLM QA accuracy), OG-RAG, Graph RAG, KG-LLM-Bench | Cited evidence for *why* the ontology layer should improve the conversational tools — strengthens LIONG-014/016 rationale | LIONG-REF-001 reading section |

One thing to skip despite looking attractive: the **IA SKOS editor / Ontology Pipeline Studio** — free license caps at 75 employees; the simulated enterprise has 800, so it would need a paid license. Protégé/VocBench (free) cover the same job.

**Not worth adding**: domain vocabularies (MeSH, AGROVOC, Getty, FIBO…), bibliographic cataloging models (BIBFRAME, FRBR, RDA), and the OWL reasoner stack — this repo validates with SHACL and doesn't use DL reasoning.

Yes, but for a filtered subset — not the catalog. Here's my reasoning.

`LIONG-011` §7 already has the right shape for this: optional components, each with "License observed", "Capability", and an "Add only when" condition, backed by research references in §16. Adding to that section is cheap and honest as long as every row ties to an open gate. Adding speculative tools inflates the version/license assessment burden the register imposes (DEC-046), and DEC-041 commits to a minimal foundation.

**Worth adding to §7 (3–4 rows):**

| Component | Why it earns a row | Gate it serves |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Neo4j neosemantics (n10s)** | RDF/SHACL handling inside the property-graph server — this is the literal mechanism for the ontology→LPG projection your `guideline_to_map_ontology_to_LPG` folder describes | OI-09 (physical graph mapping); gate = version compatibility with the pinned Neo4j release |
| **SSSOM (spec + sssom-py)** | Standard format for the "reviewed mappings" the whole source strategy depends on, with provenance built in | OI-13 (mapping artifacts) |
| **qSKOS** | Concrete, computable quality checks for any candidate taxonomy — supports the "reviewed" in reviewed mappings | LIONG-005 source assessment and OI-13 |
| **Skosify** (maybe) | SKOS conversion/cleanup; only if a candidate vocabulary needs reshaping before assessment | same as above |

**Keep out of the tool section, park in REF-001 instead:** registries (BARTOC, LOV, LOD Cloud — they're discovery aids, not components), the KG-LLM papers (reading that justifies LIONG-014/016), Skosmos/WebVOWL (UI candidates belong in LIONG-014), and the standards (ISO 25964, Z39.19, SKOS-Thes — construction methods for the guideline folder, not tools).

**Deliberately skip:** Oxigraph (a third graph server works against DEC-041; Jena/Fuseki already covers RDF serving), Morph-KGC/RML engines (only relevant if you build an RDF feed path, which the Neo4j-projection design avoids), and RDF-star (a modeling question for LIONG-006/007, not a tool — worth one assessment row against the existing record-version pattern, nothing more).

So: my recommendation is a small PR that adds ~3 rows to LIONG-011 §7 with their research references, plus the shortlist of standards/papers/registries as new rows in `LIONG-REF-001` §2 with "Assess for MVP" direction. Nothing gets selected; every row keeps the existing gate language.

---

**Prompt:**

> I am building a governed People Graph ontology for a workforce domain (an "Employee 360" model). Help me find published, reusable ontologies and vocabularies I could build on instead of inventing terms.
>
> The domain concepts I need coverage for are:
> - **Person / employment**: person identity, employment records, appointments, transfers, manager/reporting-line relationships
> - **Organizational structure**: org units, positions, posts, role/job profiles, reporting hierarchy
> - **Skills and occupations**: skills, competencies, skill levels, role-requirement mappings, skill inference (e.g., ESCO, O*NET, CTDL-ASN class solutions)
> - **Performance and decisions**: review cycles, assessments, ratings, feedback, check-ins, goals and goal progress, promotion cases and outcomes, talent-review/calibration placements, low-performance flags and follow-up actions
> - **Learning**: courses, certifications, credentials
> - **Evidence and provenance**: claims, assessments as distinct observations, evidence lines, versioned records, temporal validity (e.g., PROV-O, SEPIO-class solutions)
>
> For each candidate you find, report:
> 1. Name, maintainer, and stable URL
> 2. Format (RDF/OWL/SKOS, other) and roughly how many concepts
> 3. Which of my domain concepts it covers (map to the list above — partially is fine)
> 4. License and reuse terms as stated by the publisher
> 5. Whether it's maintained/used in production or a paper-only artifact
> 6. An honest note on fit for a workforce/people domain, and anything awkward about mappable-to-property-graph use
>
> Search these ground first: BARTOC, Linked Open Vocabularies (LOV), LOD Cloud, BioPortal (for assessment/evidence patterns), OBO Foundry, O*NET / ESCO / CTDL ecosystem, schema.org, and FIBO (for patterns only — different domain). Also look for published HR / workforce / talent ontologies and papers (search terms: "HR ontology ontology OWL", "workforce ontology", "competency ontology", "organizational ontology OWL", "skills taxonomy linked data").
>
> Rules: only suggest artifacts that are published and inspectable — no vendor marketing pages or paywalled slides. Prefer standards-aligned, openly licensed, actively maintained items. If two candidates overlap, note which is the better base. If a domain gap has no good published solution, say so explicitly — that tells me what I must model myself.

Here's what the TinyFish pass (10 searches + targeted page fetches) turned up, verified where possible and honestly flagged where not. I cross-checked each against `LIONG-REF-001` so you can see what's new.

## Already in your register — no action

| Candidate | Status in register |
| --- | --- |
| **PROV-O**, **SEPIO**, **OWL-Time**, **SKOS**, **CTDL-ASN**, **CTDL** (later scope), **Web Annotation** | Listed, with gates |
| **ESCO** (3k occupations, 13,939 skills), **O*NET** (approved scaffold, DEC-013), **NICE**, **DOL** | Skills ground, already assessed/approved scope |
| **W3C ORG** — org units, posts, membership, reporting lines | "Assess for MVP" — and this search confirms it's still the best *base* for org structure; nothing better surfaced |
| **PSDO** | The only published artifact that touches performance summaries/feedback-display concepts (DEC-055) |

## New candidates this search found

| Candidate | Maintainer / URL | Format & size | What it covers | License (as found — two still need publisher verification) | Maintenance | Fit + LPG note |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **ECO — Evidence & Conclusion Ontology** | OBO Foundry; github.com/evidenceontology — **CC0-1.0 verified today**; last push 2026-07 | OWL artifact (eco.owl/obo), evidence + assertion-method branches, production-sized | Evidence *types* supporting assertions, and whether a human or machine made the statement | CC0 (verified) | Actively maintained; used in production by GO, Monarch, others | Direct pattern for "assessment as evidence behind a claim" and man-vs-machine assessor typing. Cross-domain (biological curation) — same caveat SEPIO has. Maps to LPG as a small class vocabulary; low risk |
| **CCO — Common Core Ontologies** (esp. Agent Ontology) | commoncoreontology.github.io, on GitHub | Modular mid-level OWL suite: agents (persons + organizations + roles), qualities, information artifacts | Person/organization/role foundations | **License still to verify** (the repo moved; API 404s) | Maintained web presence, FOIS 2024 paper, cited by NIST | Strong *pattern* source for employee/org/role semantics. BFO-grounded and heavy — adopt patterns, not wholesale import |
| **Core-O** — Competence Reference Ontology | purl.org/coreo; FOIS 2024 (Calhau et al.), in LOV | OntoUML reference model **plus OWL artifact** | Competences, human capabilities, learning/professional ecosystems | To verify | Recent research artifact, cited ~11 | Modern, competency-questions-first design — closest published start for your skill-competency layer. Young; check stability before building on it |
| **LRMI** — Learning Resource Metadata Initiative | DCMI (dublincore.org/about/lrmi) | Extends schema.org for educational resources | Courses, learning resources, education levels | Publisher terms to verify (extends schema.org) | Active under DCMI | Your "learning/certifications" connector; pairs with CTDL for credentials. Web-centric schema — few concepts, not an ontology proper |
| **ResumeRDF** | rdfs.org/resume-rdf; DERI Galway | RDF/XML spec, small | Work experience, education, skills, certifications from a CV | "Creative Commons License" stated on spec page; exact variant unverified | **Stale** (2002–2006, SpecGen-era) | Useful as an example of CV/employment-term modeling only; too unmaintained to build on — take patterns, not the artifact |
| **schema.org** Person / EmployeeRole / Organization / JobPosting | schema.org | ~800 types, ~1,500 properties, web vocabulary | Person identity, employment-type roles, org links | Terms licensing per publisher docs — verify variant | Actively maintained (Google/MS/Yahoo consortium) | Good for web-exposed profiles; shallow semantics for employment records. Fine at the margin of the graph, not its spine |

## Overlap verdicts

- **Org structure**: keep **ORG** as the base (CCE + CCO's Agent Ontology as pattern sources).
- **Person identity**: **FOAF** remains the lightweight standard (in catalog, not yet in your register — worth one row); schema.org/CCO are heavier alternates.
- **Evidence typing**: **ECO** (lightweight class vocabulary, CC0, production-proven) complements the SEPIO bounded pilot rather than competing — evidence *type* vs evidence *graph*.
- **Competency modeling**: **Core-O** is the best modern starting point; ESCO/CTDL-ASN remain the *content* sources.

## Gaps — no published solution exists (model it yourself)

The search found **nothing** published for: promotion cases/nominations with outcomes, talent-review/calibration placements, mid-year check-ins, goal (V2MOM/OKR) progress tracking, low-performance flags and PIP/PEP follow-up lifecycles, and calibration sessions. That's real confirmation of what LIONG-006 must own. PSDO covers only the performance-summary/display edge of that territory.

## Next step

The new rows worth adding to `LIONG-REF-001` §2: **ECO** (Assess for MVP; cross-domain caveat, CC0 verified), **CCO Agent Ontology** (Assess patterns; license gate open), **Core-O** (Assess; artifact license + stability gate), **LRMI** (Assess for MVP), **FOAF** (lightweight person identity), **ResumeRDF** (reference patterns only; stale). Want me to add those six through the normal PR?
Please go ahead. I alos wants use to create a running list of all published ontology we will be using in this project.

I'll do both: add the six as register rows, and create a dedicated running-list document that tracks every published ontology/vocabulary the project touches, with use-status per item. Starting on a branch:

## Findings

### 1. Registry omits vocabularies it says it tracks

**Defect kind:** Incomplete inventory. The registry says it lists the published ontologies, vocabularies, and standards the project touches. It has no rows for SKOS-Thes or DCMI Terms, though the consolidated register lists both as vocabulary candidates. It also names schema.org in its coverage map and LRMI row without giving schema.org its own artifact row.

**Affected locations:** `LIONG_Design_Document_Package/REDACTED.md:15, 55, 67`; root and package copies of `LIONG-REF-001_Consolidated_Reference_Register.md:35, 38, 50`; `LIONG_Design_Document_Package/README.md:42`.

**How it can pass review while wrong:** A reviewer can confirm the six new candidates appear in both documents and see the README promise, without comparing the rest of the register against the running list. Users then treat an incomplete list as the complete inventory. Add rows for the missing artifacts with the statuses and gates from the register.

### 2. Coverage map omits modeled gaps

**Defect kind:** Coverage map omission. The performance row names promotion cases, talent-review placement, check-ins, and calibration, but omits goal progress and follow-up lifecycles. LIONG-006 defines `GoalProgress` at line 76 and includes the related review and conversation concepts at lines 99-117. LIONG-004 and LIONG-REG-001 also describe performance follow-up at lines 109 and 271.

**Affected locations:** `LIONG_Design_Document_Package/REDACTED.md:70`; `LIONG_Design_Document_Package/LIONG-006_People_Ontology_and_Canonical_Domain_Model.md:76, 99-117`; `LIONG_Design_Document_Package/LIONG-004_Competency_Questions_and_Data_Requirements.md:109`; `LIONG_Design_Document_Package/LIONG-REG-001_Assumptions_Decisions_and_Open_Questions.md:271`.

**How it can pass review while wrong:** A reviewer can verify that a performance row exists and that several named concepts match LIONG-006, then miss the omitted concepts. Later readers may conclude the map covers the modeled gaps when it does not. Name goal progress and follow-up lifecycles in the map, and state clearly which source document models each.

### 3. Combined standards row gives candidates an in-scope status

**Defect kind:** Conflicting assessment status. The registry combines RDF 1.2, RDFS, Turtle, and JSON-LD 1.1 under “In scope as standards.” The register says RDF 1.2 is under assessment with no adoption implied, and JSON-LD is an MVP assessment candidate. The combined status obscures those separate states.

**Affected locations:** `LIONG_Design_Document_Package/REDACTED.md:50`; root and package copies of `LIONG-REF-001_Consolidated_Reference_Register.md:36-37`.

**How it can pass review while wrong:** A reviewer can read “as standards” as a harmless grouping and confirm that RDF formats are used, while missing that the same status cell also covers two items still under assessment. Split the row by artifact and use each register status.

### 4. Register date predates its current revision

**Defect kind:** Stale document metadata. LIONG-REG-001 is version 0.27 and its change history says it records the November 8 search pass, but its document-control date remains November 7.

**Affected locations:** `LIONG_Design_Document_Package/LIONG-REG-001_Assumptions_Decisions_and_Open_Questions.md:9, 446`.

**How it can pass review while wrong:** A reviewer can check the new history entry and version number without checking the document-control header. Readers may then use the header date as the date of the current revision. Update it to November 8.
